title: Month-over-month change

WITH m AS (
    SELECT DATEFROMPARTS(YEAR(MovementDate), MONTH(MovementDate), 1) AS MonthStart,
           SUM(MovementValue) AS Total
    FROM retail_inventory.StockMovements
    GROUP BY DATEFROMPARTS(YEAR(MovementDate), MONTH(MovementDate), 1)

SELECT MonthStart, Total,
       LAG(Total) OVER (ORDER BY MonthStart)         AS PrevMonth,
       Total - LAG(Total) OVER (ORDER BY MonthStart) AS Change
FROM m
ORDER BY MonthStart;

    SELECT p.Region, p.WarehouseName, SUM(e.MovementValue) AS TotalMovementValue,

)

FROM t
WHERE rn <= 3
ORDER BY Region, rn;

title: Monthly rank of suppliers
q: For each month, rank suppliers by their total movement value that month and show only the top supplier (ties included).
sql:
WITH m AS (
    SELECT MONTH(e.MovementDate) AS MonthNo, d.SupplierName, SUM(e.MovementValue) AS Total,
           RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY MONTH(e.MovementDate) ORDER BY SUM(e.MovementValue) DESC) AS rnk
    FROM retail_inventory.StockMovements AS e
    JOIN retail_inventory.Suppliers AS d ON d.SupplierID = e.SupplierID
    GROUP BY MONTH(e.MovementDate), d.SupplierID, d.SupplierName
)
SELECT MonthNo, SupplierName, Total
FROM m
WHERE rnk = 1
ORDER BY MonthNo;

title: Repeat stock movements within N days
q: Find stock movements that happened within @Days days of the same warehouse's previous stock movement. Use @Days = 145. Show warehouse, previous date, current date and gap.
sql:
DECLARE @Days int = 145;

WITH v AS (
    SELECT WarehouseID, MovementID, MovementDate,
           LAG(MovementDate) OVER (PARTITION BY WarehouseID ORDER BY MovementDate, MovementID) AS PrevDate
    FROM retail_inventory.StockMovements
)
SELECT WarehouseID, PrevDate, MovementDate,
       DATEDIFF(day, PrevDate, MovementDate) AS GapDays
FROM v
WHERE PrevDate IS NOT NULL
  AND DATEDIFF(day, PrevDate, MovementDate) <= @Days
ORDER BY WarehouseID, MovementDate;
how: LAG finds the previous stock movement and DATEDIFF measures the gap. A variable makes the window easy to change. Repeat-activity checks like this are a common interview question.

title: Constraint vs trigger vs app
q: Write a query that shows, for each table, how many PK, FK, UNIQUE, CHECK and DEFAULT constraints it has.
sql:
SELECT OBJECT_NAME(parent_object_id) AS TableName,
       SUM(CASE WHEN type = 'PK' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS PK,
       SUM(CASE WHEN type = 'F'  THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS FK,
       SUM(CASE WHEN type = 'UQ' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS UQ,
       SUM(CASE WHEN type = 'C'  THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS CK,
       SUM(CASE WHEN type = 'D'  THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS DF
FROM sys.objects
WHERE type IN ('PK', 'F', 'UQ', 'C', 'D')
  AND SCHEMA_NAME(schema_id) = 'retail_inventory'
GROUP BY parent_object_id
ORDER BY TableName;
how: Prefer declarative constraints: they are faster, always applied, and help the optimizer. Use triggers only for cross-table rules, and application checks for friendly messages.

title: Stock movement chain for one warehouse
q: Starting from warehouse 1's first stock movement, use a recursive CTE to walk forward through that warehouse's stock movements in date order, with a step number.
sql:
WITH Ordered AS (
    SELECT MovementID, MovementDate,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY MovementDate, MovementID) AS rn
    FROM retail_inventory.StockMovements
    WHERE WarehouseID = 1
), Chain AS (
    SELECT MovementID, MovementDate, rn, 0 AS Step
    FROM Ordered
    WHERE rn = 1
    UNION ALL
    SELECT o.MovementID, o.MovementDate, o.rn, c.Step + 1
    FROM Ordered AS o
    JOIN Chain AS c ON o.rn = c.rn + 1
)
SELECT MovementID, MovementDate, Step
FROM Chain
ORDER BY Step;
how: The anchor picks the starting row. The recursive part finds the next row (rn + 1) one step at a time. The same shape walks hierarchies such as org charts or bills of materials.

title: MAXRECURSION
q: Generate numbers 1 to 200 with a recursive CTE. (The default limit is 100 levels.)

FROM N

title: Month-over-month with a calendar
q: For all 12 months of 2024 (even empty ones), show total movement value, previous month's total and growth %.
sql:
WITH Months AS (
    SELECT CAST('2024-01-01' AS date) AS m
    UNION ALL
    SELECT DATEADD(month, 1, m) FROM Months WHERE m < '2024-12-01'
), Totals AS (
    SELECT mo.m, ISNULL(SUM(e.MovementValue), 0) AS Total
    FROM Months AS mo
    LEFT JOIN retail_inventory.StockMovements AS e
           ON e.MovementDate >= mo.m AND e.MovementDate < DATEADD(month, 1, mo.m)
    GROUP BY mo.m
)
SELECT m AS MonthStart, Total,
       LAG(Total) OVER (ORDER BY m) AS PrevTotal,
       CAST(100.0 * (Total - LAG(Total) OVER (ORDER BY m))
            / NULLIF(LAG(Total) OVER (ORDER BY m), 0) AS decimal(6,1)) AS GrowthPct
FROM Totals
ORDER BY m;

title: Org-chart style hierarchy with path
q: Build a small hierarchy in a table variable (region head > team > warehouse) and list it with a recursive CTE, showing each level and a path like Head > North > Olivia.
sql:
DECLARE @Org TABLE (NodeID int, ParentID int NULL, NodeName nvarchar(100));
INSERT INTO @Org VALUES (0, NULL, N'Head');
INSERT INTO @Org
SELECT DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY Region), 0, Region
FROM retail_inventory.Warehouses
GROUP BY Region;
INSERT INTO @Org
SELECT 100 + p.WarehouseID, r.NodeID, p.WarehouseName
FROM retail_inventory.Warehouses AS p
JOIN @Org AS r ON r.NodeName = p.Region
WHERE p.WarehouseID <= 6;

WITH Tree AS (
    SELECT NodeID, NodeName, 0 AS Lvl, CAST(NodeName AS nvarchar(400)) AS PathText
    FROM @Org
    WHERE ParentID IS NULL
    UNION ALL
    SELECT o.NodeID, o.NodeName, t.Lvl + 1,
           CAST(t.PathText + N' > ' + o.NodeName AS nvarchar(400))
    FROM @Org AS o
    JOIN Tree AS t ON o.ParentID = t.NodeID
)
SELECT NodeID, Lvl, PathText
FROM Tree
ORDER BY PathText;

title: Age in years done right

DECLARE @Born date = '1990-12-31';

SELECT d.AsOf,
       DATEDIFF(year, @Born, d.AsOf)
         - CASE WHEN DATEADD(year, DATEDIFF(year, @Born, d.AsOf), @Born) > d.AsOf
                THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS AgeYears,

title: Average days between stock movements per warehouse
q: For warehouses with 2 or more stock movements, show the average number of days between consecutive stock movements.
sql:
WITH v AS (
    SELECT WarehouseID,
           DATEDIFF(day,
                    LAG(MovementDate) OVER (PARTITION BY WarehouseID ORDER BY MovementDate),
                    MovementDate) AS Gap
    FROM retail_inventory.StockMovements

FROM v
WHERE Gap IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY WarehouseID
ORDER BY AvgGapDays, WarehouseID;

q: Create a system-versioned table retail_inventory.PriceList that automatically keeps the history of price changes.
sql:
CREATE TABLE retail_inventory.PriceList (
    ProductID int NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY,
    Price        decimal(12,2) NOT NULL,
    ValidFrom datetime2 GENERATED ALWAYS AS ROW START NOT NULL,
    ValidTo   datetime2 GENERATED ALWAYS AS ROW END   NOT NULL,
    PERIOD FOR SYSTEM_TIME (ValidFrom, ValidTo)
)
WITH (SYSTEM_VERSIONING = ON (HISTORY_TABLE = retail_inventory.PriceListHistory));

SELECT name, temporal_type_desc
FROM sys.tables
WHERE name LIKE 'PriceList%';

title: MERGE: sync a staging table
q: Sync product prices from a staging list: update prices that changed, insert new products, and report each action.
sql:
DECLARE @Stage TABLE (ProductID int, ProductName nvarchar(80), SKU varchar(20), UnitCost decimal(12,2));
INSERT INTO @Stage VALUES
    (1,  N'Acetaminophen 325mg tablet', 'HOME-00001', 0.09),   -- price change
    (2,  N'Acetaminophen 500mg tablet', 'HOME-00002', 0.10),   -- no change
    (51, N'Loratadine 10mg tablet',     'HOME-00051', 0.12);   -- new

MERGE retail_inventory.Products AS t
USING @Stage AS s
   ON t.ProductID = s.ProductID
WHEN MATCHED AND t.UnitCost <> s.UnitCost THEN
    UPDATE SET t.UnitCost = s.UnitCost
WHEN NOT MATCHED BY TARGET THEN
    INSERT (ProductID, ProductName, SKU, UnitCost)
    VALUES (s.ProductID, s.ProductName, s.SKU, s.UnitCost)
OUTPUT $action AS ActionTaken, inserted.ProductID, deleted.UnitCost AS OldCost, inserted.UnitCost AS NewCost;
how: MERGE does insert, update and (optionally) delete in one statement. The extra `AND t.UnitCost <> s.UnitCost` skips rows that did not change. $action in OUTPUT reports what happened to each row. MERGE must end with a semicolon.

title: Generate test rows with a set
q: Insert 20 test stock movements for warehouse 1 in one statement, one per day starting 2025-01-01, with IDs 1001-1020.
sql:
WITH N AS (
    SELECT TOP (20) ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY (SELECT NULL)) AS n
    FROM sys.all_objects
)
INSERT INTO retail_inventory.StockMovements
    (MovementID, WarehouseID, MovementReference, MovementCategory, Status, MovementValue,
     MovedUnits, MovementDate, MovedAt, RecordedAt, ProductID, SupplierID, Direction)
SELECT 1000 + n, 1, CONCAT(N'RET-TEST-', n), 'A', 'Open', 100, 1,
       DATEADD(day, n - 1, CAST('2025-01-01' AS date)),
       DATEADD(day, n - 1, CAST('2025-01-01 09:00' AS datetime2(3))),
       DATEADD(day, n - 1, CAST('2025-01-01 09:01 +00:00' AS datetimeoffset(3))), 1, 1, 'IN'
FROM N;

SELECT COUNT(*) AS TestRows, MIN(MovementDate) AS FirstDate, MAX(MovementDate) AS LastDate
FROM retail_inventory.StockMovements
WHERE MovementID BETWEEN 1001 AND 1020;

title: Isolation levels
q: Name SQL Server's transaction isolation levels and the problem each one prevents. Show the current level.
sql:
SELECT CASE transaction_isolation_level
         WHEN 1 THEN 'READ UNCOMMITTED' WHEN 2 THEN 'READ COMMITTED'
         WHEN 3 THEN 'REPEATABLE READ'  WHEN 4 THEN 'SERIALIZABLE'
         WHEN 5 THEN 'SNAPSHOT' END AS IsolationLevel
FROM sys.dm_exec_sessions

title: Joins that multiply rows
q: Show each warehouse's total stock movement movement value and number of Open stock movements. Make sure the movement value is not double counted.
sql:

       ISNULL(ch.TotalMovementValue, 0) AS TotalMovementValue,
       ISNULL(op.OpenStockMovements, 0) AS OpenStockMovements
FROM retail_inventory.Warehouses AS p

           FROM retail_inventory.StockMovements

title: Short-circuit is not guaranteed
q: Return products where the name has a space and the text before the first space is longer than 8 characters. Write it safely so CHARINDEX never gives a negative length.
sql:
SELECT ProductName
FROM retail_inventory.Products
WHERE CASE WHEN CHARINDEX(' ', ProductName) > 0
           THEN LEN(LEFT(ProductName, CHARINDEX(' ', ProductName) - 1))
           ELSE 0
      END > 8;
how: SQL Server does not promise to evaluate AND conditions left to right, so `CHARINDEX(...) > 0 AND LEN(LEFT(... - 1)) > 8` could still error on a row with no space. A CASE expression controls the order. This is a senior-level detail.

title: NOT IN and the NULL trap
q: Interview trap: show why NOT IN fails when the list contains NULL. Find stock movements that are not a parent of any other stock movement, first with NOT IN (wrong), then with NOT EXISTS (right).
sql:
SELECT
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM retail_inventory.StockMovements AS e
   WHERE e.MovementID NOT IN (SELECT ParentMovementID
                               FROM retail_inventory.StockMovements)) AS NotIn_Wrong,
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM retail_inventory.StockMovements AS e
   WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM retail_inventory.StockMovements AS c
                     WHERE c.ParentMovementID = e.MovementID)) AS NotExists_Right;
how: ParentMovementID is NULL on every row here. `x NOT IN (..., NULL)` is never true, so NOT IN returns 0. NOT EXISTS ignores the NULLs and correctly finds that no stock movement is a parent. You can also fix NOT IN by adding `WHERE ParentMovementID IS NOT NULL` inside the subquery.

title: Second-highest per group
q: For each stock movement type, find the second-highest distinct movement value using a correlated subquery.
sql:
SELECT t.MovementCategory,
       (SELECT MAX(e.MovementValue)
        FROM retail_inventory.StockMovements AS e
        WHERE e.MovementCategory = t.MovementCategory
          AND e.MovementValue < (SELECT MAX(x.MovementValue) FROM retail_inventory.StockMovements AS x
                          WHERE x.MovementCategory = t.MovementCategory)) AS SecondHighest
FROM (SELECT DISTINCT MovementCategory FROM retail_inventory.StockMovements) AS t
ORDER BY t.MovementCategory;
how: For each type: find the max, then the max below it. Window functions (DENSE_RANK = 2) are the modern alternative; knowing both shows depth.

title: Running total with a correlated subquery
q: Show stock movements in ID order with a running total of movement values, without window functions.
sql:
SELECT e.MovementID, e.MovementValue,
       (SELECT SUM(x.MovementValue)
        FROM retail_inventory.StockMovements AS x
        WHERE x.MovementID <= e.MovementID) AS RunningTotal
FROM retail_inventory.StockMovements AS e
ORDER BY e.MovementID;
how: Each row sums all rows up to itself. It works on old versions but re-reads the table for every row (O(n²)); SUM() OVER is much faster. Interviewers ask this to see if you know the trade-off.

title: Rank without window functions

FROM retail_inventory.Products AS m

title: StockMovements after a warehouse's first Pending one
q: For each warehouse who has a Pending stock movement, count how many of their stock movements happened after their first Pending stock movement.
sql:

       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM retail_inventory.StockMovements AS e
        WHERE e.WarehouseID = p.WarehouseID
          AND e.MovementDate > (SELECT MIN(e2.MovementDate) FROM retail_inventory.StockMovements AS e2
                                 WHERE e2.WarehouseID = p.WarehouseID AND e2.Status = 'Pending')) AS LaterStockMovements
FROM retail_inventory.Warehouses AS p

title: IN vs EXISTS vs JOIN
q: Return warehouses with at least one Pending stock movement three ways (IN, EXISTS, JOIN with DISTINCT). Each should return the same count.
sql:
SELECT
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM retail_inventory.Warehouses
   WHERE WarehouseID IN (SELECT WarehouseID FROM retail_inventory.StockMovements
                       WHERE Status = 'Pending')) AS ViaIn,
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM retail_inventory.Warehouses AS p
   WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM retail_inventory.StockMovements AS e
                 WHERE e.WarehouseID = p.WarehouseID AND e.Status = 'Pending')) AS ViaExists,
  (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT p.WarehouseID)
   FROM retail_inventory.Warehouses AS p
   JOIN retail_inventory.StockMovements AS e ON e.WarehouseID = p.WarehouseID
   WHERE e.Status = 'Pending') AS ViaJoin;
how: All three give the same answer. A plain JOIN repeats a warehouse for each matching stock movement, which is why DISTINCT is needed. IN and EXISTS never duplicate rows.

title: Products priced above their group's average
q: Products come in families (the first word of the name, e.g. 'Ibuprofen'). List products that cost more than the average of their own family.
sql:
SELECT m.ProductName, m.UnitCost
FROM retail_inventory.Products AS m
WHERE m.UnitCost > (SELECT AVG(x.UnitCost)
                    FROM retail_inventory.Products AS x
                    WHERE LEFT(x.ProductName, CHARINDEX(' ', x.ProductName) - 1)
                        = LEFT(m.ProductName, CHARINDEX(' ', m.ProductName) - 1))
ORDER BY m.ProductName;
how: The family is computed with LEFT + CHARINDEX (text before the first space). The correlated subquery averages only products of the same family.
